title: Integer multiplication: schoolbook vs Karatsuba
problem_statement: Given two non-negative integers a and b, each written with exactly n digits in base B = 2^15 as little-endian digit lists (index 0 = least significant digit), compute the product a*b as a little-endian list of exactly 2n base-B digits (high-order digits may be zero).

input.parameter: n = number of base-2^15 digits of each factor.
input.size_measure: 2n digits (30n bits). Costs count single-word digit operations: every intermediate value stays below 2^31, so each digit operation is O(1). Since n digits = 15n bits, the exponents are the same in bit complexity.

algorithms.name: schoolbook (long) multiplication
algorithms.idea: Multiply a by each digit of b and add the shifted partial products, propagating carries row by row.
algorithms.pseudocode: res = [0]*(2n); for i: carry = 0; for j: t = res[i+j] + a[i]*b[j] + carry; res[i+j] = t mod B; carry = t div B; res[i+n] = carry
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) digit operations (exactly n^2 multiply-adds on every input)
algorithms.correctness: Distributivity: a*b = sum_i a_i B^i b. Invariant: after row i, res holds (a_0 + ... + a_i B^i) * b. Each t = res + a_i b_j + carry is at most B^2 - 1, so every stored digit is < B and every carry is < B.

algorithms.name: Karatsuba
algorithms.idea: Split each factor into a low and a high half. Three half-size products (low*low, high*high, and |x1-x0|*|y1-y0|) suffice instead of four, because x0*y1 + x1*y0 = x0*y0 + x1*y1 - (x1-x0)(y1-y0). Recurse; below 32 digits use schoolbook.
algorithms.correctness: Karatsuba & Ofman 1962. The identity above holds over the integers, so the recombined result equals x*y. The subtractive form (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 2, 4.3.3) keeps all three sub-products the same size, giving T(n) = 3 T(ceil(n/2)) + Theta(n) = Theta(n^log2(3)) by the master theorem. The 32-digit base-case cutoff changes constant factors only.

relationship: Both polynomial. Karatsuba lowers the exponent from 2 to log2(3) ~ 1.585. It was the first sub-quadratic multiplication algorithm. The line continues with Toom-Cook (n^(1+eps) for any fixed eps > 0; Knuth TAOCP Vol. 2, 4.3.3), Schoenhage-Strassen 1971 (O(n log n log log n)) and Fuerer 2007, and ends at Harvey-van der Hoeven 2021 (O(n log n) bit operations on a multitape Turing machine).

sources.title: Multiplication of many-digital numbers by automatic computers
sources.note: No DOI. English translation in Soviet Physics Doklady 7 (1963), 595-596.

sources.title: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2: Seminumerical Algorithms (3rd ed.)
sources.note: Section 4.3.3 (how fast can we multiply?), including the subtractive form of Karatsuba's identity used here.

sources.authors: Harvey, D.; van der Hoeven, J.
sources.title: Integer multiplication in time O(n log n)

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree on random, carry-stress and maximal-digit inputs and match an independent big-integer oracle (Python's built-in product, used only in harness.check). V2 (since 2026-10-06, RESEARCH_LOG RL-056): the measured quantity is the exact number of DIGIT MULTIPLICATIONS performed by the unchanged implementations, counted by an int-like digit type (CountingDigit in harness.py) that propagates through the carry and borrow arithmetic. On n = 64..2048 (powers of two, so no padding occurs): schoolbook = n^2 exactly; Karatsuba (cutoff 32) = 3^(log2(n/32)) * 32^2 exactly (e.g. 248832 at n = 1024). Both fits give alpha = 1.000 at tolerance 0.02, and each algorithm's rival is rejected: Karatsuba's counts against n^2 give alpha = log2(3)/2 = 0.792, schoolbook's against n^log2(3) give 2/log2(3) = 1.262. The earlier timing fit could not reject n^2 for Karatsuba (deviation analysis F2, research/2026-10-07b_deviations.md). Additions are not counted.

caveats: Exact counts of digit multiplications, not of all digit operations. The cutoff (32 digits) changes constants only. Fast algorithms after Karatsuba (Schoenhage-Strassen, Harvey-van der Hoeven) are stated in bit complexity on a multitape Turing machine, not in word operations.
notes: Python's own int multiplication itself switches from schoolbook to Karatsuba above a size threshold, which is why the implementations here work on explicit digit lists instead. O(n log n) is conjectured to be optimal for integer multiplication, but no matching unconditional lower bound is known.
